A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChannelTokenFormer research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting experiments, ablations, missingness tests, scalability measurements, and spectral analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds comparator results and an empirical visualization of patch embeddings under missingness.

M1.justification: FFT-guided patching, channel tokens, patch masking, attention restrictions, decoding, and the training objective remain unchanged. New Algorithm 1 documents the existing tokenization and masking procedure rather than introducing a new component.

E1.justification: The six practical datasets and five conventional benchmarks are retained. The ETT1/EPA experiments now called discrete missingness still use the previously reported 5–20-step zero-filled gaps; v2 Tables 19–20 correspond to v3 Tables 16–17. The new embedding visualization remains within existing ETT1 missingness coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds TimeFilter and DUET to the main practical comparisons, conventional benchmarks, and ETT1 short-gap comparison. It also adds FreTS and FITS across the six practical datasets in Table 18. ContiFormer is removed from the SolarWind missingness comparison but retained for EPA, substantially revising comparator coverage.

E3.justification: New Figure 10 introduces a controlled comparison of ETT1 patch embeddings with no injected missingness versus 30% missingness, visualized using t-SNE. Existing forecasting horizons, metrics, training budgets, and documented missing-gap lengths remain unchanged. The newly stated exclusion of drop-last is additional disclosure, not an established protocol revision.

E4.justification: Appendix C.6 adds a tokenizer-level robustness analysis showing near-overlap of clean and corrupted patch embeddings. Existing component ablations, masking-strategy comparisons, scalability tests, and modified-TimeXer analysis are retained. The short-gap forecasting analyses are relocated and extended with comparators rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed error bars in Appendix E while their reproducibility statements say three seeds; this inconsistency persists unchanged. Added comparator columns follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice, with no new statistical procedure or reported increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Substantial comparator results are added and ContiFormer’s SolarWind results removed. New TimeFilter results alter rankings: Weather CMSE/CMAE are 0.273/0.293 versus unchanged CTF values of 0.275/0.296. Retained practical-result cells are unchanged. Conventional results also change: Crossformer’s ETTh2/192 CMSE is corrected from printed 177 to 0.877, while SimpleTM’s ETTh1 average changes from 0.422/0.428 to 0.443/0.436 despite unchanged constituent scores.

T1.justification: The forecasting loss, attention mathematics, and Appendix B spectral derivations retain their substance. Revised notation and Algorithm 1 restate existing procedures. The new discussion of approximately Lipschitz-continuous tokenizers provides a heuristic explanation, without a new formal assumption, bound, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and central unified-framework contribution remain unchanged. Empirical-superiority wording in Section 5.1 narrows from best on all datasets to best or second-best, and from outperforming all baselines to most baselines. The conclusion strengthens the scalability qualification by explicitly requiring additional mechanisms for thousands of channels.

C2.justification: v3 adds a smooth-tokenizer explanation for discrete-missingness robustness and further justification for the downsampled practical benchmarks. It expands the interpretation of interpolation-induced frequency bias and specifies channel sparsification or grouping as scaling remedies. Quadratic attention costs and MSE-related amplitude attenuation were already acknowledged in v2.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds pseudocode, explicitly states that drop-last is not used, and supplies a code-repository link with pointers to hyperparameters and patch lengths. v2 only promised a future code release. v3’s final reproducibility statement still retains that future-release wording, so the availability statements are inconsistent.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted positioning against DUET, TimeFilter, FreTS, and FITS, plus citations concerning fair benchmarking and Lipschitz robustness. These additions update the discussion of dependency modeling and frequency-based approaches without replacing the existing related-work framework or novelty positioning.

P1.justification: v3 condenses the problem formulation, revises notation and introductory explanations, adds focused appendix subsections, and moves short-gap experimental details into Appendix C.6. Publication headers and acknowledgments are added. Most prose and the overall section hierarchy remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the t-SNE figure, frequency-baseline table, and algorithm display, and expands comparison tables with additional columns. Existing masking, missingness, and forecasting displays are relocated or renumbered; the principal architecture and spectral figures remain unchanged. The visual format is retained, although expanded tables become denser.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons, more qualified performance statements, and explicit pseudocode/code access modestly improve evaluation and transparency. These benefits outweigh limited new reporting problems: Table 19 misassigns ETTh1 averages, and Appendix C.6’s blanket superiority statement conflicts with Tables 16–17. The method and most existing evidence remain unchanged, while the three-versus-five-seed inconsistency persists, limiting the overall gain.
